title: Grit
author: Angela Duckworth
blurb: Psychologist Angela Duckworth asks why some people achieve so much more than others with similar ability. Her answer is grit, a blend of passion and perseverance for a long-term goal. Drawing on her research with West Point cadets, spelling bee finalists, salespeople and students, she shows that grit often predicts success better than talent or test scores. She argues that talent matters, but effort counts twice: once in building skill and again in turning skill into achievement. Gritty people tend to share four traits. They have a deep interest, they practice deliberately, they feel a sense of purpose, and they hold on to hope after setbacks. Duckworth's encouraging message is that grit is not fixed. It can be grown from the inside, and also from the outside through supportive parents, challenging activities and cultures that value persistence.

lessons.t: Why Talent Isn't the Whole Story
lessons.b: At West Point, a simple grit score predicted which cadets would survive brutal summer training better than their talent-based admission scores did.

lessons.b: Effort turns talent into skill and then turns skill into achievement, so it matters twice as much as talent alone.
Lasting interest rarely arrives as a sudden spark; it grows slowly through exploration, then deepens as we keep discovering new things in the same field.

The narration's contrast with people drifting away is shown only as a text label; nothing in the drawing shows it. (fix: Move the label left so it has at least 24px of padding inside the panel. Add a small figure or two fading or walking away from the books, with the label placed under them.)

lessons.t: Practice That Actually Makes You Better
lessons.b: Experts improve through deliberate practice: targeting a specific weakness, working on it with full focus, getting feedback, and repeating.
